There have been discussions about various quality of life improvements for the repo on Zulip and GitHub, so I’m creating this thread so we can centralise the discussion a little more. Here are some examples (feel free to link below any ones I’ve not included):

  • adding skills and automated reviews (here)
  • adding a review dashboard, and various other things to make reviewing easier (see this big issue with many links to other work in progress)
  • better handling for references in the repo and website).

There are also a few things I’ve been thinking about working on, e.g

  • comparator integration (for example, as a stretch goal having automation to easily do a comparator check for formal proofs submitted by people). This might be something we work on at the workshop.
  • setting up and maintaining a branch of the repo with formal proofs that are too large to fit in main

It seems like quite a few people are interested in working on this sort of stuff, so let’s coordinate!
Feel free to also suggest ideas here:)
cc @Will Blair, @Yaël Dillies, @Moritz Firsching, @Daniel Chin, @Franz Huschenbeth, etc!

Thanks for organizing this, some of my thoughts:

  • Comparator. leanprover/lean-eval is great existing infrastructure. Authors mark trusted statements with @[eval_problem], and the tooling generates one comparator workspace for each problem, with Challenge, Solution and config.json. We already produce that kind of metadata from our attributes withextract_names, so this could be relatively easy to integrate.

  • Skills and review. I can take a first pass at this based on your comments on #4876.

  • Large proofs. FC is already on Reservoir. Would pinned Lake packages work as well as a branch, without the Mathlib version drift a long-lived branch collects?

I probably have mentioned these in passing, but stating them here again. I've also been busy with other stuff lately so there might have progress/discussion on these topics already that I missed. I'm also typing this at 1AM my time so this could very well devolve into rambling.

Verification and review of lean generated proofs
Lots of people are submitting links to a proof in their own repo as novel solutions. For simple solutions, these PRs are pretty easy to review, but for complicated lean proofs that range anywhere from 5k-20k lines of code, it's borderline impossible to review. I would love for a system to ingest a github link and be able to verify that it builds properly, checks to see if the axiom dependencies are minimal, and no crazy hypotheses are assumed. A caveat here is that the lean proofs from the usual Erdos Problems folks are usually just a single file, so it's very easy to pop it into Lean Web and confirm it compiles with no errors. Many proofs people are submitting via links in PRs are multi-file proofs because their LLM of choice decided that that's a cleaner way of organizing the code (which it is), but also makes it more difficult to verify in Lean Web.

Centralization of proofs
@Paul Lezeau mentioned this above as a separate branch to accept long form proofs. I'd probably argue this might even be a separate repo that gets maintained. The main problem with people submitting links to lean proofs is that almost none of them are kept up to date with mathlib versioning. Boris actually does a good job with his repo regarding this, but I don't think it's expected that most people will hold that standard. So this brings up the problem how of do we verify some of these proofs in a year or so when were multiple mathlib versions ahead and the lean proof doesn't compile. Having a centralized repo of long proofs and having some maintainer keep versioning up to date is the only long term solution I see.

Lean to LaTeX Converter
There's been a good chunk of PRs recently of links to lean proofs with a PR description of what the code is supposed to do. It's great if we can make sure the code compiles without error, but it's still difficult to grok at the code and figure out what's going on especially in 20k line repo. There was some discussion on the Erdos Problems website I think between Thomas and Boris about how they've been converting lean generated proofs into a LaTeX code block so the mechanisms of the proof are more human readable. I think this could also help with the review process for the more complicated proofs.

More than happy to work on these at the workshop.

Will Blair said:

  • Comparator. leanprover/lean-eval is great existing infrastructure. Authors mark trusted statements with @[eval_problem], and the tooling generates one comparator workspace for each problem, with Challenge, Solution and config.json. We already produce that kind of metadata from our attributes withextract_names, so this could be relatively easy to integrate.

I think integration with https://lean-lang.org/eval/ would be fantastic!

There is a few things to be taken into account here:

  1. we do want to support "either proof or disprove" for the open probems. From a technical point of view this is largely a solved problem, there are patches to comparator, which allow to either submit a proof a disprove, i.e. a proof that the statement implies False.
  2. One would have to think a little about if it can be expanded to multi-file support, because currently it seems to be focussed (because of how comparator works in its current form) on single files, but also that could be changed
  3. Definition support: not all of our problems are only Prop valued: some take a non-Prop valued answer(sorry), but here again comparator is ready it has definition support, and also our answer(sorry) mechanism can inject the corresponding definitions.

We should explore if it is better to copy the infra from https://lean-lang.org/eval/ separately or contribute our problems in a form that https://lean-lang.org/eval/ can handle.
In any case I think those two projects are made for each other:

Formal Conjectures :heart: lean-eval

on a related note: https://live.lean-lang.org/ has the nice comparator integration! It might be cool to get the same thing working with Formal Conjectures, i.e. have a live.lean-lang.org where one an choose in the drop-down: "lean-v27.1.0 with mathlib and formal_conjectures"

re: skills and automated reviews: generally of course great to have! There seem already to be a bunch of people who have build these and use these, especially for formalising, which is nice! There seems to be a little less currently around reviewing, which would be equally important (and very similar of course). Perhaps some people can try out their reviewing SKILLs by applying it to pending prs?
Related are of course also the "Please solve that conjecture" SKILLs: when those are employed during review that might find misforamlisations
Happy to review and contribute there as well, will start with the pending changes by @Will Blair to our AGENT.md

Hi all,

I am nearly-on-the-verge-I-promise-real-soon-now about to do a big overhaul of LeanEval --- and now might be the right moment to consider integration.

The priority is to release a "v1" set of problems, which will then remain fixed. (Roughly, this will cut out of some of "not so great" problems in the current set, and add a big new set of problems Kevin has just given me from Annals.)

But the other goals are:

  • collect more data from contributors, i.e. about models used, compute and inference costs, level of human supervision, etc.
  • give submitters better tools to managing their submissions (e.g. updating metadata after the fact, and repairing the group a submission is filed under)
  • give more emphasis in the leaderboard results to "uniquely solved" problems
  • provide better tools for comparing solutions when there are multiple submissions, particularly making LoC and instructions or heartbeat counts public information
  • provide a "recent solutions" page showing recent newly solved problems
  • add a new "software verification" problem set (initially this will be in "draft mode", i.e. no fixed set of problems), which will essentially be a "second tab" besides "maths formalization".

This suggests the possibility of integrating formal conjectures as another tab... (I think it's important to keep it separate from the main "maths formalization" group, which is meant to be for problems with known informal solutions.)

However to do this (if it is even at all desirable) I would really need external help. I am trying to juggle a lot of balls at the moment, and lean-eval keeps slipping behind other things. (@Vasily Ilin has already offered to help me, which sounds wonderful, but I have not even been finding the time to coordinate with him.)

Great! A few thoughts.
(1) Just a reminder that Formal Conjectures also contains the formalisation of many theorems where an informal proof is known: https://google-deepmind.github.io/formal-conjectures/browse/?category=research+solved In some cases for those the formal proof is in the repo and in some cases we link a formal proof via our "formal_proof using foo at bar" mechanism, but the majority, i.e. about 1000 theorem statement lack a recorded formal proof and some of them would make good candidate for lean-lang eval, from papers/arxiv or conjectures that are mentioned in wikipdia.

(2) Although a first version doesn't need even for our open conjectures, it I think it would be also great for the statements on lean-lean eval that have an informal proof to allow disproving. This will make it easier to automatically find misformalisations.
The patch to comparator that allow just that is ready to go, see this branch for an example:
https://github.com/augustepoiroux/comparator/blob/upstream/disproofs/tests/projects/disproof_valid/Solution.lean for an example. it hasn't been upstreamed yet and I don't know if @Auguste Poiroux and @Henrik Böving are already in conversation about it or if there is a Zulip thread somewhere. There are some subleties about universes here, @Eric Wieser has also been thinking about it, if I remember correctly.

(3) definitions support (i.e. allow in the solution to provide an answer) is upstreamed and we have patched our answer(sorry) mechanism to work with it. Although this doens't affect many problems.

(4) multifile support, i.e. having not just one Challenge.lean file, but rather allowing imports is also something that would make integration of Formal Conjectures more easy

We are most happy to help! @Will Blair https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/issues/4930 has opened this.

I think instead of copying your infra it would be much nicer to integrate our growing problem set into https://lean-lang.org/eval/ and improve it together
There were also some people coming to the upcoming workshop (6. to 11. September, organized by Kevin et. al.) who have shown interest in moving this forward
I'm also quite happy to help with Lean eval integration, and should have a fair bit of time to do so, starting next week:)
I think a good place to start would be the FC100 lists (one for solved problems, one for open problems), since the goal is that these will be frozen subsets that we will periodically release

Lean eval ought to have private solutions if I understand correctly. But if one formalises an open conjecture from Formal conjectures, the solution has to be public to make it worthwhile. So what exactly would be integrated?
I think the one of the main benefits of the integration would be infrastructure here, e.g. having a submission system integrated into comparator, etc.
I think the differences around submission policies (e.g. when to release public solutions, etc) may be another reason for formal-conjectures to sit in a different tab.
I'm just worried that this would lead to actors solving / claiming to solve mathematically open questions but keeping the solutions to themselves.

That would also make misformalisations a bit more serious, since it may be easier to find a misformilasition and "solve" a conjecture abusing it; but without checking the submitted (private?) proofs, from the outside it would still look like conjecture XY is solved.
Those are both fair points. Concerning the public/private solutions, I think a release of the proof that was submitted should be part of the terms of participation
(one could also imagine a system for releasing similar to what was suggested here: #Model comparisons for Lean > LeanEval @ 💬)

Felix Pernegger said:

That would also make misformalisations a bit more serious, since it may be easier to find a misformilasition and "solve" a conjecture abusing it; but without checking the submitted (private?) proofs, from the outside it would still look like conjecture XY is solved.

I think releasing solutions partially helps with this, without fully addressing the issue that misformalisations may always occur in these types of benchmarks

@Kim Morrison , these are great goals! I am especially excited about software verification problems!

I think the most important QoL improvement is missing from your set of goals: keeping solutions private, at least for some time. Right now, it's very hard to evaluate models on LeanEval, because if web search is enabled, they can just find a leaked solution. I vote for enforcing that solutions to a given problem stay private for 1 month, and releasing all solutions at once.

Yes, I agree that for the eval problems, we have to "require" that submissions are private (in the sense that they come from a private repository; of course we can't really require that they aren't simultaneously published elsewhere, but we can ask), that are then automatically released after some time period (1 month? 2 months?).

But then if we add open conjectures into the system, I think we should do the opposite: require that submissions for these come from public repositories!

Hey all, I agree with @Paul Lezeau that FC100 sounds like a good place to start. I had started a draft FC-side adapter in #4951 following an earlier discussion. It generates one pinned LeanEval workspace from a Formal Conjectures declaration and currently handles theorem proofs, definition answers, and helper modules. I expect its structure to change as we decide where the boundary between Formal Conjectures and LeanEval should sit.

I have also updated #4930 as the coordination issue. Based on this discussion, a possible starting point is:

  • two frozen FC100 lists, one solved and one open;
  • private submissions followed by automatic release for solved problems;
  • public submissions from the start for open conjectures.

The next decision seems to be the smallest v1 submission format and which workspace-generation components should live in LeanEval. I’m happy to help implement that and adapt #4951 around the agreed design. Disproof support can follow once the Comparator work has been merged.

@Kim Morrison or @Vasily Ilin, is there an existing branch or design document for the LeanEval overhaul? Where would you prefer us to coordinate the integration work?
@Will Blair I've opened this issue here on the Lean-eval side to coordinate: https://github.com/leanprover/lean-eval/issues/533
great, thanks!

I've finally found time to write up my plan for lean-eval, see #Model comparisons for Lean > LeanEval overhaul . It includes my ideas re: FC integration, but please don't take anything as set in stone: tell me what you want instead, and I'll see if we can make it happen.

Going back to Paul's original topic, are there QoL improvements that we would like to have in preparation for the workshop in a couple of weeks? I'm starting to get some free time again and I wonder if there's any pre-work that we should try and accomplish (or even just planning) to make the workshop go smoother.

Two that come to mind are:

  • review automation: I think it would be nice if we had a way to using an LLM to do an initial review of PRs when they are opened. I think there are several components here: one is the review skills that several people (including myself) are working on, and another is thinking about the actual design of the system, and less has been done on that side (I have a few thoughts though, so happy to chat if you wanna pick up this stream)
  • another that I think would nice nice is a bot to detect and tag abandoned PRs so someone can adopt them. I think this should work as follows: after a few weeks of inactivity on the PR, the bot sends a message to ping the author, and if there’s no reply, adds (after some amount of time) a please-adopt tag
Both of these were things I was thinking of working on, but I think they could be good fits for you so happy to leave them for you if you want!
(And I think both could be useful for the workshop, particularly the first one!)

Thanks @Daniel Chin!
Just one random item: one could take a look at caching and potentially improve it: for all the library FormalConjecturesUtil ...ForMAthlib but also potentially for our verso build.
I think basically the status quo currently is that if you add a new file to ./FormalConjectures/Arxiv for example not touching anything in FormalConjecturesForMathlb it it currently takes ~45 min until the CI gives feedback, but it probably should be doable in ~5min?

Created an issue here: FC#5113
Other thing that may be worth looking into: depending on Tau-Ceti (I think this will unlock a bunch of conjecture statements!)

I think there is a lot we can learn from the broader ecosystem as well, then deciding which we can copy/integrate/adapt (like we've been doing recently with LeanEval). For instance, while prototyping a review skill, I found this useful repo from TauCeti Review
Ah yeah, the build time was driving me crazy as well. I can do some investigation on that.
